claim: Dorsoventrality in leaves depends on the pre-patterned expression of KANADI and HD-ZIPIII genes within the plant shoot apical meristem (SAM).
source: Dorsoventrality in leaves has been shown to depend on the pre-patterned expression of KANADI and HD-ZIPIII genes within the plant shoot apical meristem (SAM).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work, as indicated by the passive voice 'has been shown'.

claim: Asymmetric auxin levels within initiating leaves have been proposed to help establish leaf polarity.
source: However, it has also been proposed that asymmetric auxin levels within initiating leaves help establish leaf polarity, based in part on observations of the DII auxin sensor.
evidence: The claim references a proposal from prior work based on DII auxin sensor observations.

claim: There is no obvious asymmetry in auxin levels during Arabidopsis leaf development based on R2D2 auxin sensor analysis.
source: By analyzing and quantifying the expression of the R2D2 auxin sensor, we find that there is no obvious asymmetry in auxin levels during Arabidopsis leaf development.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from R2D2 auxin sensor analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mDII control sensor exhibits an asymmetry in expression in developing leaf primordia early on.
source: We further show that the mDII control sensor also exhibits an asymmetry in expression in developing leaf primordia early on, while it becomes more symmetric at a later developmental stage as reported previously.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of mDII expression patterns presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mDII control sensor becomes more symmetric at a later developmental stage.
source: We further show that the mDII control sensor also exhibits an asymmetry in expression in developing leaf primordia early on, while it becomes more symmetric at a later developmental stage as reported previously.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and references to prior reports.

claim: The results argue against the importance of auxin asymmetry in establishing leaf polarity.
source: Together with other recent findings, our results argue against the importance of auxin asymmetry in establishing leaf polarity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented and other recent findings.

claim: Mature leaves of seed plants are usually flat with distinct cell types making up their dorsal (upper) and ventral (lower) tissues.
source: The mature leaves of seed plants are usually flat with distinct cell types making up their dorsal (upper) and ventral (lower) tissues, which are derived from the adaxial (side closest to meristem) and abaxial (side farthest from meristem) primordium tissues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about plant leaf anatomy.

claim: Dorsal and ventral leaf tissues are derived from the adaxial and abaxial primordium tissues.
source: The mature leaves of seed plants are usually flat with distinct cell types making up their dorsal (upper) and ventral (lower) tissues, which are derived from the adaxial (side closest to meristem) and abaxial (side farthest from meristem) primordium tissues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about plant developmental biology.

claim: Dorsoventral leaf patterning is derived from a pre-pattern present in the shoot apical meristem (SAM).
source: Recently, we reported evidence in support of a previously proposed hypothesis that dorsoventral leaf patterning is derived from a pre-pattern present in the shoot apical meristem (SAM), where leaves arise (Hagemann and Gleissberg, 1996; Husbands et al., 2009; Kerstetter et al., 2001; Koch and Meinhardt, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' recent work and prior hypotheses from cited literature.

claim: Transcription factors that promote dorsal and ventral leaf cell types are expressed in the SAM in a pre-pattern that determines the orientation of the leaves that subsequently form.
source: We found that transcription factors that promote dorsal and ventral leaf cell types are expressed in the SAM in a pre-pattern that determines the orientation of the leaves that subsequently form (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: The plant hormone auxin promotes dorsal cell fate by maintaining expression of the Class III HD-ZIP transcription factor REVOLUTA (REV) and repressing KANADI1 (KAN1) expression in the adaxial cells of organ primordia.
source: Additionally, we found that the plant hormone auxin promotes dorsal cell fate by maintaining expression of the Class III HD-ZIP transcription factor REVOLUTA (REV) and repressing KANADI1 (KAN1) expression in the adaxial cells of organ primordia (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: Exogenous auxin application to tomato leaf primordia resulted in the formation of radialized leaves that appeared ventralized.
source: This conclusion was based in part on the finding that exogenous auxin application to tomato leaf primordia resulted in the formation of radialized leaves that appeared ventralized.
evidence: The claim references findings from prior work that informed a previous conclusion.

claim: The DII auxin sensor indicates low levels of auxin in adaxial leaf tissues compared to abaxial tissues at leaf initiation.
source: Also, it was found that an auxin sensor, the DII (Brunoud et al., 2012; Vernoux et al., 2011) indicates low levels of auxin in adaxial leaf tissues compared to abaxial tissues at leaf initiation (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim references findings from cited prior work.

claim: Asymmetries in auxin concentrations between the adaxial and abaxial tissues in leaf primordia, as a result of PIN1 mediated auxin transport, were proposed to help establish leaf dorsoventral cell type patterning.
source: Hence asymmetries in auxin concentrations between the adaxial and abaxial tissues in leaf primordia, as a result of PIN1 mediated auxin transport, were proposed to help establish leaf dorsoventral cell type patterning (Qi et al., 2014), in contrast to the proposed pre-pattern mechanism (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim references a proposal from cited prior work.

claim: Low levels of auxin in adaxial primordium tissues are necessary to restrict the expression of the WOX1 and PRS genes to the middle domain.
source: Building further on this conclusion, a more recent study proposed that low levels of auxin in adaxial primordium tissues are necessary to restrict the expression of the WOX1 and PRS genes to the middle domain, since auxin promotes their expression (Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim references a proposal from cited prior work.

claim: Auxin promotes the expression of WOX1 and PRS genes.
source: Building further on this conclusion, a more recent study proposed that low levels of auxin in adaxial primordium tissues are necessary to restrict the expression of the WOX1 and PRS genes to the middle domain, since auxin promotes their expression (Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim references findings from cited prior work.

claim: The reported asymmetry in auxin has been linked to asymmetries in the mechanical properties of leaf tissues and their morphogenesis.
source: Finally, the reported asymmetry in auxin has also been linked to asymmetries in the mechanical properties of leaf tissues and their morphogenesis (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim references findings from cited prior work.

claim: A high DII/mDII ratio indicates relatively low levels of auxin sensing.
source: A high DII/mDII ratio indicates relatively low levels of auxin sensing while a high mDII/DII ratio indicates relatively high levels of auxin sensing (Liao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the established properties of the R2D2 sensor from cited work.

claim: A high mDII/DII ratio indicates relatively high levels of auxin sensing.
source: A high DII/mDII ratio indicates relatively low levels of auxin sensing while a high mDII/DII ratio indicates relatively high levels of auxin sensing (Liao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the established properties of the R2D2 sensor from cited work.

claim: During early stages of leaf development, DII/mDII ratios were extremely low in cells coinciding with high levels of PIN1-GFP expression.
source: In general, during these early stages DII/mDII ratios were extremely low in cells coinciding with high levels of PIN1-GFP expression while on either side of these cells, ratios were higher but to a similar degree (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: On either side of cells with high PIN1-GFP expression, DII/mDII ratios were higher but to a similar degree.
source: In general, during these early stages DII/mDII ratios were extremely low in cells coinciding with high levels of PIN1-GFP expression while on either side of these cells, ratios were higher but to a similar degree (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: REV expression can coincide with PIN1 at later stages when it expands peripherally.
source: Previously, by examining PIN1-CFP together with pREV::REV-2xYPet and pKAN1::KAN1-2xGFP in similarly staged primordia we found that REV expression can coincide with PIN1 at later stages when it expands peripherally but that KAN1 expression is invariably complementary to cells with high PIN1 expression (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: KAN1 expression is invariably complementary to cells with high PIN1 expression.
source: Previously, by examining PIN1-CFP together with pREV::REV-2xYPet and pKAN1::KAN1-2xGFP in similarly staged primordia we found that REV expression can coincide with PIN1 at later stages when it expands peripherally but that KAN1 expression is invariably complementary to cells with high PIN1 expression (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: KAN1 expression is associated with low auxin sensing cells.
source: Overall our observations therefore indicate that KAN1 expression is associated with low auxin sensing cells while REV expression is associated with different levels of auxin sensing depending on the stage of development.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of DII/mDII ratios and gene expression patterns.

claim: REV expression is associated with different levels of auxin sensing depending on the stage of development.
source: Overall our observations therefore indicate that KAN1 expression is associated with low auxin sensing cells while REV expression is associated with different levels of auxin sensing depending on the stage of development.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of DII/mDII ratios and gene expression patterns.

claim: At 3DAS, the expression patterns of REV and KAN1 are already polar within leaf primordia.
source: At 3DAS, the expression patterns of REV and KAN1 are already polar within such primordia, although the FILAMENTOUS FLOWER (FIL) expression domain at this stage of development is still being refined (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: The FILAMENTOUS FLOWER (FIL) expression domain at 3DAS is still being refined.
source: At 3DAS, the expression patterns of REV and KAN1 are already polar within such primordia, although the FILAMENTOUS FLOWER (FIL) expression domain at this stage of development is still being refined (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: At 3DAS, PIN1 is polarized towards the distal tip of leaf primordia.
source: At this stage, PIN1 is polarized towards the distal tip of leaf primordia but has reversed polarity away from the primordia, towards the meristem, in cells adjacent to primordia on the adaxial side.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of PIN1 expression patterns.

claim: At 3DAS, PIN1 has reversed polarity away from the primordia, towards the meristem, in cells adjacent to primordia on the adaxial side.
source: At this stage, PIN1 is polarized towards the distal tip of leaf primordia but has reversed polarity away from the primordia, towards the meristem, in cells adjacent to primordia on the adaxial side.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of PIN1 expression patterns.

claim: According to the R2D2 sensor, DII/mDII ratios varied from moderate to high in adaxial cells of the primordia at 3DAS.
source: According to the ratio-metric auxin sensor R2D2, DII/mDII ratios varied from moderate to high in adaxial cells of the primordia but also varied similarly in abaxial regions - indicating no obvious asymmetry between the two tissue types (Figure 2A to C and M-N; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: According to the R2D2 sensor, DII/mDII ratios varied similarly in abaxial regions at 3DAS.
source: According to the ratio-metric auxin sensor R2D2, DII/mDII ratios varied from moderate to high in adaxial cells of the primordia but also varied similarly in abaxial regions - indicating no obvious asymmetry between the two tissue types (Figure 2A to C and M-N; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: A low DII/mDII ratio was found consistently in more distal regions towards the tip of the primordia and in the provasculature at 3DAS.
source: A low DII/mDII ratio was only found consistently in more distal regions towards the tip of the primordia and in the provasculature, matching the overall pattern of signal from PIN1-GFP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of R2D2 ratios.

claim: The low DII/mDII ratio pattern matches the overall pattern of signal from PIN1-GFP.
source: A low DII/mDII ratio was only found consistently in more distal regions towards the tip of the primordia and in the provasculature, matching the overall pattern of signal from PIN1-GFP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing R2D2 ratios with PIN1-GFP expression.

claim: The variability in DII/mDII ratios within adaxial and abaxial tissues was clearly apparent from the distal to proximal end of the initiating leaves.
source: By carefully monitoring DII/mDII ratios from the distal to proximal end of the initiating leaves, the variability in DII/mDII ratios within adaxial and abaxial tissues was clearly apparent (Figure 2D–L and O–S, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: The same overall pattern of R2D2 signal was found in 28 out of 28 leaves examined at 3DAS and 4DAS.
source: This same overall pattern of signal was found in 28 out of 28 leaves that were examined each for 3DAS and 4DAS (14 seedlings each).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data across multiple samples.

claim: High levels of auxin sensing (mDII/DII) were only found in the more distal regions towards the tip of the primordia and within the provasculature, where PIN1-GFP was expressed.
source: Lastly, by inverting the ratio and visualizing the mDII/DII (high ratio intensity corresponding to high cellular auxin sensing), we could further confirm that high levels of auxin sensing were only found in the more distal regions towards the tip of the primordia and within the provasculature, where PIN1-GFP was expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The DII pattern showed an asymmetry of expression in leaf primordia at 3 DAS, indicating relatively low auxin levels in adaxial primordium cells.
source: In contrast to the R2D2 pattern, the DII pattern showed an asymmetry of expression in leaf primordia at 3 DAS, indicating relatively low auxin levels in adaxial primordium cells, as found previously.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of DII expression and references to prior findings.

claim: DII signal appeared strongest in the adaxial epidermis at 3DAS.
source: DII signal appeared strongest in the adaxial epidermis but was also stronger in the adaxial sub-epidermal cell layer compared to abaxial epidermal and sub-epidermal cell layers (Figure 4- A, C, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (n = 18/18 leaves, nine seedlings).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and supplement.

claim: DII signal was stronger in the adaxial sub-epidermal cell layer compared to abaxial epidermal and sub-epidermal cell layers at 3DAS.
source: DII signal appeared strongest in the adaxial epidermis but was also stronger in the adaxial sub-epidermal cell layer compared to abaxial epidermal and sub-epidermal cell layers (Figure 4- A, C, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (n = 18/18 leaves, nine seedlings).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and supplement.

claim: One day after 3DAS, DII signal started to show increased relative expression in the abaxial epidermal and sub-epidermal layers compared to earlier stages.
source: One day later, DII signal started to show increased relative expression in the abaxial epidermal and sub-epidermal layers compared to earlier stages (n = 14/14 leaves, seven seedlings) (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Expression of the mDII marker was higher in the adaxial cells of leaf primordia at 3DAS.
source: Surprisingly we found that, like the DII results, expression of the mDII marker was also higher in the adaxial cells of leaf primordia at 3DAS (n = 16/16 leaves, eight seedlings) (Figure 4-B,D,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and supplement.

claim: The mDII marker expression pattern appeared almost identical to the DII marker pattern except that the mDII marker also exhibited high levels of expression in the shoot meristem whereas the DII sensor did not.
source: The pattern appeared almost identical to the pattern found using the DII marker except that the mDII marker also exhibited high levels of expression in the shoot meristem whereas the DII sensor did not (compare Figure 4-A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing DII and mDII expression patterns in figures.

claim: At 4DAS, both DII and mDII markers started to show expression on the abaxial side with no obvious asymmetry in their expression.
source: The similarity of expression between DII and mDII was also apparent at 4DAS when both markers started to show expression on the abaxial side as well with no obvious asymmetry in their expression (n = 20/20 leaves, 10 seedlings) (Figure 4H-Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4 and supplement.

claim: Treatment with 5 mM NAA resulted in a strong decrease in DII expression compared to mDII.
source: To verify the auxin sensitivity of the sensors used we imaged seedlings before and after treatment with 5 mM NAA and found a strong decrease in DII expression compared to mDII and an increase in the mDII-tdTom/DII-V ratio for the R2D2 sensor, consistent with an increase in auxin levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from auxin treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Treatment with 5 mM NAA resulted in an increase in the mDII-tdTom/DII-V ratio for the R2D2 sensor, consistent with an increase in auxin levels.
source: To verify the auxin sensitivity of the sensors used we imaged seedlings before and after treatment with 5 mM NAA and found a strong decrease in DII expression compared to mDII and an increase in the mDII-tdTom/DII-V ratio for the R2D2 sensor, consistent with an increase in auxin levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from auxin treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Abaxial tissues have a slightly larger proportion of cells with high DII/mDII ratios (low auxin sensing) with a mean of 0.29; standard deviation, SD (0.24); standard error of mean, SEM (0.01) compared to adaxial tissues, which have a mean ratio of 0.24, SD (0.20), SEM (0.004).
source: According to the data, abaxial tissues have a slightly larger proportion of cells with high DII/mDII ratios (low auxin sensing) with a mean of 0.29; standard deviation, SD (0.24); standard error of mean, SEM (0.01) compared to adaxial tissues, which have a mean ratio of 0.24, SD (0.20), SEM (0.004) (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of R2D2 data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The Area Under the Curve (AUC) measure of similarity for aggregated adaxial and abaxial nuclei DII/mDII ratios was found to be 0.556.
source: The Area Under the Curve (AUC) measure of similarity was found to be 0.556, which again indicates that the distributions are overall very similar (0.5 would indicate they are identical) (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The relative levels of auxin sensing in adaxial and abaxial tissues in young leaf primordia are overall very similar.
source: All together our results demonstrate that the relative levels of auxin sensing in adaxial and abaxial tissues in young leaf primordia, are overall, very similar.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the quantitative analysis of R2D2 data.

claim: A larger proportion of cells in abaxial tissues display higher DII to mDII ratios compared to adaxial tissues, indicating slightly higher levels of cellular auxin sensing in adaxial tissues.
source: The small difference we identify is that a larger proportion of cells in abaxial tissues display higher DII to mDII ratios compared to adaxial tissues, indicating slightly higher levels of cellular auxin sensing in adaxial tissues, which is the opposite conclusion to that reported earlier (Guan et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the quantitative analysis of R2D2 data and contrasts with prior reports.

claim: High levels of auxin sensing are found in presumptive provascular cells that also express high levels of PIN1-GFP.
source: In this study, we find high levels of auxin sensing in presumptive provascular cells that also express high levels of PIN1-GFP.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of R2D2 ratios and PIN1-GFP expression.

claim: PRS expression is not restricted to cells with high PIN1-GFP expression, although they are both in the middle domain.
source: In fact simultaneous imaging of PIN1-GFP together with PRS-GFP in young leaf primordia indicates that PRS expression is not restricted to cells with high PIN1-GFP expression, although they are both in the middle domain (reconstructed transverse optical section; Figure 4E of (Caggiano et al., 2017)).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: If auxin is applied exogenously, WOX1 and PRS do not become expressed ectopically.
source: More significantly, it was shown that if auxin is applied exogenously, WOX1 and PRS do not become expressed ectopically (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: The data argue against a role for auxin in limiting WOX1 and PRS expression to the middle domain.
source: Overall then, our data argue against a role for auxin in limiting WOX1 and PRS expression to the middle domain.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data and prior findings.

claim: The adaxially expressed HD-ZIPIII genes restrict auxin response, thereby limiting WOX1 and PRS expression to the middle domain whether the level of auxin in adaxial cells is high or not.
source: Rather, they support previous results indicating that, like the ventrally expressed KANADI and Auxin Response Factor genes (ARF2, ARF3 and ARF4), the adaxially expressed HD-ZIPIII genes restrict auxin response, thereby limiting WOX1 and PRS expression to the middle domain whether the level of auxin in adaxial cells is high or not (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: The ventrally expressed KANADI and Auxin Response Factor genes (ARF2, ARF3 and ARF4) restrict auxin response.
source: Rather, they support previous results indicating that, like the ventrally expressed KANADI and Auxin Response Factor genes (ARF2, ARF3 and ARF4), the adaxially expressed HD-ZIPIII genes restrict auxin response, thereby limiting WOX1 and PRS expression to the middle domain whether the level of auxin in adaxial cells is high or not (Caggiano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a cited study by the authors.

claim: The findings strongly argue against the proposal that asymmetries in the distribution of auxin within young leaf primordia have a strong influence on leaf polarity.
source: In summary, our findings strongly argue against the proposal that asymmetries in the distribution of auxin within young leaf primordia have a strong influence on leaf polarity (Qi et al., 2014) or regulate tissue mechanics (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data and contrasts with prior proposals.

claim: The findings strongly argue against the proposal that asymmetries in the distribution of auxin within young leaf primordia regulate tissue mechanics.
source: In summary, our findings strongly argue against the proposal that asymmetries in the distribution of auxin within young leaf primordia have a strong influence on leaf polarity (Qi et al., 2014) or regulate tissue mechanics (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data and contrasts with prior proposals.

claim: The DII marker was used to assess relative auxin levels without direct comparison to the mDII marker in previous studies.
source: The finding that both the mDII and DII markers, when driven by the 35S promoter, are expressed in an asymmetric pattern during leaf initiation suggests that one reason our conclusions may differ from those reported earlier (Qi et al., 2014) is that previously, the DII marker was used to assess relative auxin levels without direct comparison to the mDII marker.
evidence: The claim is an inference about methodological differences between studies.

claim: The pattern of mDII expression changes rapidly over 12 hr.
source: As our time-lapse imaging shows, the pattern changes rapidly over 12 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and so a staging discrepancy can explain this difference.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The R2D2 reporter acts as a proxy for the cellular sensing of auxin.
source: In-order to investigate the proposed auxin asymmetry proposal in more detail, we decided to examine the distribution of auxin within initiating leaf primordia using the ratio-metric R2D2 reporter, which acts as a proxy for the cellular sensing of auxin (Liao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the established properties of the R2D2 sensor from cited work.
